### Observed differences

- Assignments were reshuffled across much of the process. In the earlier window, six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22) drew their work from a similar mix of resource codes in which User_105 held roughly 6–8% of assignments alongside several comparable codes; in the later window, User_98 had become the largest single code for all six activities, at about 13–20% of assignments each, while User_105 and the formerly leading codes no longer appear among the top shares. The unnamed remainder stayed at about 44–46% in both windows. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008]
- A08 and A11, which show identical assignment profiles, moved from three codes jointly holding about 37% of assignments to a new leading code, User_133, at about 17%, with the former leaders falling to about 5–7% or out of the top shares entirely. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]
- A04, which occurred in every trace in both windows, became fully concentrated on one resource: earlier it was spread across 29 distinct codes with the most-used code at 48% of events; in the later window a single code performed all observed A04 events. [CONC001]
- Control flow shifted as well: A09 appeared in about 57 in 100 traces earlier versus about 71 in 100 later. Of A05's observed outgoing transitions, the share leading to A09 rose from about 57% to 71%, while the share to A04 fell from about 44% to 29%. Of A16's outgoing transitions, the share to A11 fell from about 29% to 12%, while the share to A07 rose from about 31% to 40% and to A10 from about 11% to 16%. [OCC001, DIR001, DIR002]
- A04 also tended to sit slightly later within traces in the later window (mean relative position about 0.13 versus 0.15; event positions, not clock time). [POS001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that resource allocation changed: in the later window, work on a broad set of activities was reassigned from the resource groups that previously handled it to different groups. This involves A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, where a new group led by User_98 (about 13–20% of assignments) replaced a group that included User_105; A08 and A11, where User_133 (about 17%) became the main handler; and A04, which went from 29 distinct resources to exactly one. Supporting signs: the resource family produced 9 qualifying items where roughly 0.006 would be expected without a change, all with empirical strength near 0.9995, and the swap moves in the same direction across six activities, which random re-splitting of stable traces would not typically produce. Limitations: the A08/A11 and A13/A14 profiles are identical pairs, so the nine items reflect about seven distinct activity profiles rather than nine independent changes, and the evidence cannot show whether the swap reflects a changed assignment rule or simply a different mix of active resources in the later period. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, ASSIGN008, CONC001]

Other differences: routing and participation shifted in ways this hypothesis does not cover — A09 ran in about 57 versus 71 in 100 traces, A05 sent more of its outgoing flow to A09 and less to A04, and A16 sent less to A11 and more to A07 and A10; these four control-flow items also exceed the roughly 0.21 expected by chance in their family. A11 appears on both sides (less flow from A16, and changed assignments), but whether the routing and allocation changes are connected cannot be determined from this evidence. A04's slight positional shift is noted but does not by itself show the activity was moved. [OCC001, DIR001, DIR002, POS001]
